newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian sub-continent gold prices seen firming.
newsitem.headline: Indian sub-continent gold prices seen firming.

text.p: Gold prices in the Indian sub-continent are likely to remain firm in the near term with a major festival in India and currency devaluation in Pakistan fuelling demand, analysts said on Monday.

They said Indian demand for gold had picked up in the last few days ahead of Diwali, the festival of lights, which falls this year on November 11. Traditionally, Hindus consider Diwali the most auspicious occasion for buying gold and silver.
Gold prices on the Bombay bullion market rose 20 rupees per 10 grammes to 5,170 rupees in the week to Monday on renewed festival buying.
"Reports of a recovery in gold prices in world markets have also triggered fresh speculative interest in gold prices during the week," said Mahavir Jain, a jeweller.
Dealers in Pakistan's commercial city of Karachi said the recent steep devaluation of that country's currency against the dollar could keep gold prices firm.
Demand for gold in Dubai, the business hub of the United Arab Emirates and feeder market for the Indian sub-continent's consumption, is also expected to grow in the next two months.
Analysts said the completion of the winter harvest and the start of the wedding season could spur demand for gold in both India and Pakistan, bound by similarities in tradition.

"I expect good demand from rural areas following the harvest, besides festival buying," said bullion analyst Madhusudan Daga. A good monsoon has boosted India's hopes of a bumper harvest this year but recent cyclonic floods have damaged crops in some areas.
A cyclone in Andhra Pradesh early this month destroyed a variety of crops, dealers said. As a result, farmers in that state will have less money to spend on gold this year.

Daga said Indian bank lending rates had come down marginally by a percentage point to 17.25 percent following a liberal credit policy announced recently by the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank.
"But a funds shortage continues. Industrial recession and rising inflation are also affecing the overall demand for gold in India," said Daga.

Karachi gold prices, which rose sharply after last week's devaluation of the Pakistani rupee by 7.86 percent against the dollar, are likely to ease in the next few days before firming again, dealers said.
Gold prices, which shot up 277 rupees to 5,309 per 10 grammes after the devaluation, closed eight rupees lower at 5,301 in dull trading on Sunday.
"It is a temporary phenomenon and gold rates are likely to rise again," the dealer said.
Dubai souk traders said turnover in bullion and jewellery had taken off this month as Indian goldsmiths started importing stock in preparation for Diwali.
Indian subcontinent demand is also expected to be aided by stable bullion prices below $400 an ounce.
